# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 106 — The EMET Bible (Literal)

**Translator:** EMET | **Source:** Codex Athous, Shepherd of Hermas 106 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_106_page_001.jpg

---

## Similitude 9, Chapter 23

**1** I saw the tower and the Lord of the tower, and those who were building it, glorifying the Lord greatly. **2** And I asked the shepherd who was standing beside me, "Who is this lord of the tower?" "It is the Son of God," he answered. **3** "But these six men and the virgins with them — who are they?" "These are the holy angels of the Lord, and the virgins are the holy spirits." **4** "And the young men building the tower?" "These also are holy angels of the Lord, but the six are over them. All who build the tower shall enter into the kingdom of God. **5** But the others who brought stones — they shall enter the kingdom if they also walk in truth." **6** "And those who brought stones but did not fit them in — who are they?" **7** "These had believed but departed on account of their double-mindedness; and they were not inserted into the building because they were double-minded and full of malice. **8** They shall be excluded from the kingdom of God." **9** "But who are those round stones that fit in nowhere?" **10** "These also are those who have believed," he said, "but have great wealth in this world; and when affliction comes, on account of their riches and their business they deny the Lord." **11** I answered him: "When then shall they be fit for the building of the tower?" **12** "When," he said, "their riches, which have ensnared their souls, are cut away, then they shall be useful for the Lord. **13** Just as the round stone can only become square when something is cut away and removed from it, so those who are wealthy shall become useful to God only when their riches are cut away. **14** And you must first learn from yourself, for when you were wealthy you were useless; but now you are useful and profitable for life."

---

*EMET: the chapter repeats and reinforces the round-stone-made-square maxim with direct pastoral application to Hermas, establishing it as the central parable of wealth-renunciation.*
